items.title: Massive leak exposes 41,000 DHS workers and undercover ICE agents
items.excerpt: An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” Read full article Comments

items.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th
items.excerpt: United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company's 2026 launch schedule into oblivion. The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval. The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA's primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan. Read full article Comments

items.title: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland
items.excerpt: The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States. The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia. “It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,” Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it's being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Peptide peddlers cheer as RFK Jr. unilaterally grants access, overruling FDA
items.excerpt: Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration. The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Health Again movement, and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a "big fan." But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they're effective, and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk. Kennedy's new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register , with the final publication date set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. Kennedy had quietly proposed this rule earlier this month.…

items.excerpt: Sign up · Docs · Book demo · Website · Feature requests · Contribute · Hiring Macro is the all-in-one workspace for you and your team. It unifies email + messages + docs + tasks + agents + CRM into a single fast interface with shared team-level memory. Everything in your workspace is @linked and searchable so your team (and your agents) never have to switch tools. # Why Macro We built Macro because we wanted a single operating system for our startup. There are many good software products, and we used them all — Slack, Linear, Notion, HubSpot, and Superhuman — but they don't work together as one system. As we scaled our last venture to ~20 people things started to break: every team got their own tools and the company was held together by MCP and Zapier. The company was not computable. It was chaotic. Macro is a complete redesign of work software from the ground up as a single system. Designed by us in NYC and Toronto, dogfooded by our team of ~15 for two years. Built in SolidJS and Rust for speed and reliability. We're focused on building something that any small company or team at a larger company can use as their "operating system". # Features Macro is composed of 'blocks' designed to be modular, extensible, and work together like Lego. For each block, we studied the best prior art and tried to make it even better. items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. items.title: Prompt Injection Is Just the Start of AI Agent Security (Here's What You Need)
items.excerpt: Learn more about agent security here: https://fandf.co/4i1Qs4u My second brain helps me run my entire business, and that means giving it access to a lot of my systems and data, so I check everything it pulls in and keep its access limited. That works for one agent. A company has agents running across cloud platforms and employee devices, and IT has to know which ones exist, who owns them, and what they can reach. Microsoft is expanding Project Perception, building on Agent 365, to secure AI agents at scale. It gives agents their own identity, scopes their access to the task, and contains them as risk changes, without taking away employees' approved access. Dynamic Permissions gives agents task-specific, time-bound access to supported resources, and separately, risk-based access controls evaluate supported agent actions using current risk and policy. Your team reviews and approves protections before they're enforced. Thanks to Microsoft for working with me on this!

items.title: Anthropic Seriously Just Got Hacked Again
items.excerpt: Anthropic just got hacked again, and this time we know who did it. Cathedral, a start-up founded by former DOGE staffers and co-founded by the Pentagon's former chief data officer, ran AI agents against Anthropic under its bug bounty program. The front door held for days; the way in was business software Anthropic buys from other companies, and it led to meeting transcripts, salaries and Slack messages about its advanced models. items.title: The Worst 48 Hours in Internet History

Token-funded bounties to incentivize competition-style participation in blockchain development projects would result in wider and better allocation of investment, and allow investors to diversify exposure across a field of potentially successful projects. We propose a centralised platform for the administration of token-funded bounty driven development projects whereby experts allocate pools of invested capital according to the technical merits of development projects, and investors are rewarded with token allocation in funded projects. items.title: Compensating the victims of automation is economically beneficial
items.excerpt: It is likely that we see a wave of jobs automated away in the coming years. Already software developers, artists and mathematicians are standing at the precipice, and other careers are sure to follow. Responses range through denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. Some fight to prevent automation, others have already attempted to switch careers or focus. But few suggest that they will accept their job loss so long as it comes with a decent payout. However I believe this is likely the best option - not just for them, or just so that we can buy them off to prevent them blocking automation, but because of fundamental uncertainty about what and when different jobs will be automated. Consider someone considering studying medicine today. After 8 years of education and 3 years of residency, they hope to be able to eventually earn decent pay and work less crazy hours. By that stage they'll be hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt. They have no idea how the world might change in 11 years and they might reasonably consider that career choice too risky, and instead start earning immediately in e.g. a physical apprenticeship. This applies to numerous fields, from potential taxi drivers considering buying a car to, yes, maths and software engineering: we don't know whether AI will be able to fully replace these tasks or we'll still need numerous humans to manage and round out the AI. Absent a reliable promise of compensation if these careers go AWOL we will face fewer…

items.title: Dependencies in conversation and in software
items.excerpt: I often find myself frustrated and overwhelmed when people try to explain things to me. It's similar to the guy in this Software engineer interns on their first day be like... video, but with me it's more like "Software engineer after 12 years be like...". At a high level, the conversations I'm referring to look something like this: Eric: Here is how A works. Eric: Here is how B works. Eric: Here is how C works. Adam: Um — Eric: Here is how D works. Adam: But — Eric: Here is how E works. Adam: I — Eric: Here is how F works... In this example, B depends on A. In order to understand B, you have to first understand A. When Eric tried to explain B to me, I didn't understand A yet. Without understanding A, I wasn't ready to hear an explanation of how B works. Ideally , before explaining B, Eric would have checked in to see if I understand A. Only once I understand A do we have the green light to proceed. JavaScript A thought occurred to me the other day: this situation seems analogous to software dependencies. Consider the following JavaScript code: [1] // b.js import { a } from 'a'; const result = a + 2; export { result }; b.js depends on a . Without a , b.js isn't able to run. In order for b.js to run, there needs to be a node_modules directory with an a package. Something like this: b.js node_modules/ a/ package.json index.js Suppose you want to run b.js but see that node_modules is missing a . You can run npm install a to download the dependency. items.title: Borrow My Accordion?
items.excerpt: In 2005 I bought an accordion on eBay for $38 (plus $42 shipping) . It arrived surprisingly in tune, but I made up for that by playing it badly. It sat next to my bed in the Fishbowl, a large triple I shared with David and Lucas sophmore year: I didn't really know what I was doing, but enjoyed trying to play Scotland the Brave as loudly as possible while holding down a bass button to simulate drones. Pretty quickly my friends confiscated it under the excuse that one of them (Jules?) wanted to learn to play. This was actually very kind, because accordion ergonomics don't suit me: they reliably hurt my wrists. This started a pattern that has continued for the last 20 years: anytime the accordion comes back from loan I try to get it out again as quickly as possible before I wishful thinking myself into deciding to play it. I think the only maintenance it's had has been people replacing the broken straps and case, and while it leaks a little air it's in surprisingly good shape. Here's my uncle playing it for morris dancing at our wedding : Ever since I was eleven I've had one big dream about my wedding: that there would be Morris dancing. So, we're planning to have pick-up Morris at the break in the contra dance. Davy has agreed to play accordion. By my count, we have about sixteen possible dancers. items.title: Three Villages in a Trenchcoat, Post I
items.excerpt: Epistemic Status: 15 years working as a therapist, 6+ of them with rationalist and EA clients. 9 years teaching and directing at rationality camps and workshops, as well as being a member of several of this community's overlapping subcultures. Disclaimer: I finished my first draft of this article and its two subsequent ones months ago and sent them out for feedback to various people before a bunch of stuff happened in my life that derailed me from finishing, and in the meantime a big ol' brouhaha started around Slutcon 2 and various frictions this article was meant to highlight within the rationalist and EA community surfaced in The Discourse. All of which is to say this post isn't about any particular incident, but the underlying dynamics that make many of them arise. When I make claims about how things go wrong and why, I'm drawing on a mix of research, observations, and both clinical and non-clinical experiences within these communities and beyond them. TL;DR : It's helpful to think of the rationality/EA community as a village (social scene, professional network, dating pool, housing market, all tied together by shared culture and communal events), but it's also ultimately misleading. items.title: Your Book Review: The Ghost In My Brain
items.excerpt: [ This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] In 1999, Professor Clark Elliott is rear-ended by a stranger at a stoplight. He’s shaken but figures he’s fine, and drives to work. Spoiler: Clark Elliott is not fine. Elliott is severely concussed, and this fact will dictate the next ten years of his life. Elliott’s memoir is based on notes he took while concussed. Reading it is like watching someone try to troubleshoot their broken laptop using the broken laptop. In the opening chapter, Elliott describes walking from his office to his car after a long winter workday: “At this point my world had collapsed inward on itself… I looked down at my feet and shouted at myself to walk, but I knew it was hopeless. I had lost the mysterious initiative that impels us all forward when we walk, and I knew that without brain rest I wouldn’t be getting it back. I considered lying down in the snow.” Over an hour later, Elliott finally manages to cross the parking lot and begins the second phase of his trial: getting into the car. “I’d lost the concept of center. items.title: Why Global Trepanation?
items.excerpt: A friend asked me to investigate the following mystery: why do 5-10% of skulls from 10,000 BC to 3,000 BC, all over the world, have holes in them? Why do bone growth patterns indicate that most skull-hole-havers survived years after their holes were drilled, even though brain surgery today requires careful sterilization (and frequently, prophylactic antibiotics) to prevent fatal infections? And why did everyone stop doing this sometime around the beginning of recorded history? Was it cultural diffusion? No. Trepanation (the technical term for drilling a hole in the skull) was common across Europe and South America, with scattered cases in Africa and other continents. The Old and New Worlds had limited contact after about 10,000 BC, and most customs don’t survive for five thousand plus years with no reason. Was it good medicine? Sort of, but not in a way that entirely solves the mystery. Trepanation is an effective treatment for epidural hematoma: a patient ruptures a blood vessel in their skull, filling the cranial cavity with blood, and the pressure rises so high that it squashes various vital blood vessels and brain regions, killing the patient. Drilling a hole in the skull releases the blood, relieves the pressure, and saves the patient’s life. This is great, but these kinds of hematomas are very rare today: about 1/100,000 per year. items.title: How the UAE got too powerful to punish
items.excerpt: This is why the UAE bought an English football club Sudan’s civil war has become one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises — and evidence increasingly points to the United Arab Emirates as a crucial backer of the RSF. In this episode, I follow an investigation that used TikTok videos, satellite imagery, cell phone data, and interviews with former fighters to trace a secret supply network through Libya. The trail leads to weapons, vehicles, mercenaries, and ultimately powerful figures in Abu Dhabi. I also look at how the UAE built enough influence through business, investment, and football to make Western governments reluctant to confront it. This is the story of how soft power can protect hard power — even in the middle of a devastating war. So if you want a privacy first VPN, my viewers gets 25% off at https://obscura.com/SEARCHP or scan the QR code for only $6/month This video explains how Jared Kushner’s post–White House business empire has become entangled with foreign governments that once dealt with him as a U.S. official. It uses Albania as the clearest case study, where Kushner-linked companies have pursued major resort projects on Sazan Island and at Zvërnec with extraordinary help from the government of Edi Rama. Those projects sit at the intersection of disputed land ownership, protected environments, strategic-investor laws, and longstanding concerns about corruption in Albania. The video argues that these deals create a serious conflict: foreign governments can potentially help or hurt Kushner’s private interests while he remains deeply connected to U.S. foreign policy and the Trump administration. And in Albania, that relationship is now producing a backlash, as protesters use the Kushner projects to challenge a much broader system of political favoritism and corruption. Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. I contrast a stopwatch view, on which time saved is whatever the clock records, with a ledger view, on which it is a counterfactual that has to be read next to the errors the work lets through, and I argue for the latter. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. I give a baseline model of checking in which, until the model is good enough not to check, a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on how good the model is; checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate; and over-trust buys minutes on the clock at a larger cost in total minutes. I show what randomized studies can and cannot identify, and I replicate METR's developer study from its public data: the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depending on the estimand (34% without adjusting for a chance imbalance), and AI helped on somewhere between 3% and 82% of them. Finally, I restate the published record, with stated bounds in place of imported point assumptions. In GDPval's own review-every-output workflow, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x; the consultants outside the frontier were faster, and more often wrong. Last, I test two of the model's predictions in a small pre-specified experiment on AI reviewers checking AI…

items.title: Enhancing Deep Learning Model Performance through Data Generation Strategies: Classification of Olive Tree Diseases
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models are highly effective in a wide range of domains, particu larly in plant disease diagnosis. However, their performance is often limited by challenges such as insufficient data and class imbalance. In our work, we propose a comprehensive data generation strategy to overcome these limitations. First, we apply various data generation techniques, including traditional augmentation methods, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic image generation using Deep Convolu tional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs), to create new data samples. Second, we exploit this generated data in three scenarios: (S1) balancing class distribution in the original dataset, (S2) increasing the number of samples per class, and (S3) expanding the dataset while maintaining balanced classes. Third, we evaluate the impact of these data distributions (S1, S2, S3) on model perfor mance using the EfficientNetV2B0 architecture with pre-trained and fine-tuned weights. The experimental results show a substantial improvement in classifica tion accuracy, emphasizing the critical role of data diversity and class balance. These findings highlight the effectiveness and adaptability of the proposed strat egy of data generation and distribution for enhancing dataset quality, offering promising applications in plant disease detection and precision agriculture.

items.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information…

items.title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.

items.title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new…

items.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
items.excerpt: Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe , we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. Our vision: From idea to completed software The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship GitHub is…

items.title: Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents
items.excerpt: Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined. Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati , a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft , and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers . Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before. That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture. Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most: More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one. items.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
items.excerpt: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n ! As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone. The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same . However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists. Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. items.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
items.excerpt: Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: Minimize coordination Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the…

items.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
items.excerpt: AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships. To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software. Here are the tips they shared with us. Meet the Java Champions Vlad Mihalcea , founder of Hypersistence and author of the book High-Performance Java Persistence Patrick Baumgartner , software crafter at 42talents with 20+ years of Java experience Frank Delporte , senior technical writer at Azul and maintainer of Foojay.io with 15+ years of Java experience Vlad Mihalcea GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently? I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer. Loans and investments may count toward SSBCI requirements if they are from a private source as described in Section VIII.b of the Guidelines, even if that source originates outside of the United States. The transaction, including the use of the private financing, must otherwise comply with all SSBCI requirements and any other applicable state, local, or federal law, including Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) filing requirements that may be triggered (see, 31 CFR Parts 800 and 802). items.title: Hybrid sales rise while battery electric sales remain lower after tax credit expiration
items.excerpt: In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26), 23% of new light-duty vehicles sold in the United States were hybrid electric, battery electric, or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, down slightly from 24% in 3Q25. Between 3Q25 and 3Q26, hybrid electric vehicles continued to gain market share, reaching 16% of light-duty vehicle sales. Growth of hybrid electric vehicle sales has slowed this quarter as the average transaction price for a new vehicle passed $50,000-the first time this price has been reached so far this year, according to Kelley Blue Book.

items.title: U.S. small-scale solar generation has quadrupled in the last decade
items.excerpt: We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country-California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida-are in regions with more abundant solar resources. Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives.
